q: Does an Odisha aluminium smelter's captive coal power count in its CBAM figure?
title: Odisha smelter captive power and CBAM
short: Not for the CBAM charge on aluminium. Power from a captive coal plant is indirect emissions under the CBAM Regulation, and Annex II lists aluminium for direct emissions only. Anode consumption and perfluorocarbons from anode effects do count, and the captive plant's emissions still matter for buyers counting Scope 3.
audience: Primary aluminium smelters and their EU buyers in the Angul and Jharsuguda belt of Odisha

ul: CO2 from consumption of prebaked carbon anodes or Soderberg paste in the pots.
Perfluorocarbons, CF4 and C2F6, released during anode effects, converted with the GWPs set in the CBAM rules.
Fuel burnt in casthouses, anode baking and other on-site processes.
The embedded emissions of any primary aluminium bought in as a precursor.

p: The CBAM Regulation defines indirect emissions as emissions from producing the electricity consumed in production, wherever it is produced. A smelter's own coal plant next door is therefore indirect, not direct. For aluminium, iron and steel and hydrogen, Annex II limits the charge to direct emissions, so the many tonnes of CO2 per tonne of metal from coal power are not in the CBAM obligation today.

sections.h: Why you should still measure it
p: Article 30 asks the Commission to assess adding indirect emissions for these goods, and EU buyers report the full footprint in Scope 3. Keep the captive plant's coal consumption, gross and auxiliary generation and power sent to the pots, so you can show both the CBAM figure and the full footprint.
